analysis.one_liner: Treats US companies that move their headquarters abroad to dodge taxes as still American for tax purposes.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the House and referred to the Ways and Means Committee, where it has sat with no cosponsors and no action since February 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: When an American corporation is bought by, or merges into, a company organized overseas but its own former owners still control the result, it can claim it is now a foreign company and stop paying US corporate tax on its worldwide income. This bill changes the tax code's definition so many more of those deals count as American companies anyway: it raises the ownership share that triggers the rule from 60 percent to 80 percent, adds a test for companies whose executives and day-to-day management stay in the United States, and applies the rules to tax years ending after May 8, 2014. The sponsor is Rep. Lloyd Doggett; it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and has had no other action.
analysis.who_benefits: American taxpayers generally, because profits of companies that invert would keep flowing into the US tax base instead of escaping to a low-tax foreign parent. Domestic competitors who already pay full US taxes would also no longer be undercut on taxes by lookalike foreign firms.

how_it_helps.text: The bill treats a foreign corporation as domestic for tax purposes when a post-2014 acquisition gives former US shareholders more than 50 percent of its stock, closing the main path companies used to shed US tax residence while keeping American operations [S2].

It also counts companies whose executive officers and senior management are based primarily in the United States, and groups with at least 25 percent of employees, pay, assets, or income in the United States, as domestic — so moving the legal address on paper no longer escapes US tax while the actual business stays put [S2].

The changes apply to taxable years ending after May 8, 2014, meaning companies that already inverted after that date would be taxed as domestic again rather than keeping the benefits of earlier deals [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Multinational companies that have inverted or plan to, and their shareholders, who would face US corporate tax on worldwide income they currently avoid; the bill acknowledges no offsetting revenue estimates or transition relief for completed deals.

drawbacks.text: The changes are retroactive to tax years ending after May 8, 2014, so companies that completed inversions in good faith under the existing law would face new taxes on past transactions — retroactive tax changes are a standard fairness objection [S2].

The bill keeps an exception for companies with substantial business activities in their foreign country of organization, so inversions paired with genuinely large foreign operations would still escape the rule [S2].

Critics of anti-inversion rules generally argue that higher taxes on these companies can push deals in the other direction, toward foreign buyers acquiring American firms outright instead of American firms buying foreign ones [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The policy goal — keeping US-taxed profits from companies whose business and management remain in the United States — directly serves ordinary taxpayers, and the drafting closes several known escape routes, including the management-and-control test. The serious costs are the retroactivity, which taxes past deals under new rules, and the retained substantial-business-activities exception, which leaves a narrower loophole. On balance the design is more aggressive than the current law, and its main flaw is the lack of transition relief for companies that already inverted.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee in February 2026, and nothing has happened to it since — no cosponsors, no hearing, no vote — while Congress remains in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on February 11, 2026, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which handles tax legislation [S1] [S4].
No other member signed on as a cosponsor [S3].
The committee has taken no further action on the bill: the full action history lists only the introduction and the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, multinational companies that have inverted or may want to are better off, because the bill has not moved and the stricter rules have not been enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies seeking to escape US tax

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Corporate Inversions Act of 2026 and referred it to the Ways and Means Committee

sides.party_line_note: With a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors, and no votes or hearings, the record shows no pattern of support or opposition yet.

industries.industry: Multinational corporations that invert or have inverted
industries.note: These companies gain by reorganizing so a foreign parent holds the US business, lowering their US tax bill while the business itself stays American. The bill would tax them as domestic again, retroactive to tax years ending after May 8, 2014, taking away that benefit.

industries.industry: US-headquartered companies that pay full corporate tax
industries.note: Firms that never inverted compete against inverted rivals that legally pay less US tax; tightening the rules removes that tax advantage and levels the field. Their gain comes alongside higher federal revenue rather than at taxpayers' expense.

analysis.trajectory: With one sponsor, zero cosponsors, and a committee that has taken no action in months, this bill is very likely to sit in the Ways and Means Committee until the Congress ends without a hearing or vote — the fate of most single-sponsor tax bills.
